texts.orig: Abstract
texts.text: Abstract

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Background: Acute  appendicitis  is  common  and  time-critical,  yet  reliable  differentiation  between uncomplicated and complicated disease at first contact remains challenging, particularly where imaging access  and  senior  review  vary. Objective: To  determine  whether  serum  direct  hyperbilirubinemia functions  as  an  early  indicator  of  complicated  appendicitis  and  to  clarify  its  role  within  routine preoperative assessment. Methods: We conducted a prospective study in the emergency surgery unit at Minia  University  Hospital,  enrolling  400  consecutive  patients  with  clinical  features  of  acute appendicitis. Patients were classified as uncomplicated or complicated (perforated/gangrenous) using operative  and  histopathological  criteria.  Preoperative  assessment  included  clinical  evaluation  and routine laboratories, with direct bilirubin measured alongside standard indices. Diagnostic performance was estimated using receiver operating characteristic analysis with area under the curve (AUC) and threshold-based accuracy. Results: Higher direct bilirubin values were associated with complicated appendicitis.  Direct  bilirubin  showed  good  accuracy  (AUC:  0.71,  CI:  0.64-0.79,  p<0.001*)  with  a cutoff  >0.39  mg/dL  yielding  72%  sensitivity  and  51%  specificity.  Interpreted  with  vital  signs  and routine laboratory markers, bilirubin added selective, adjunctive information for early risk stratification. Conclusion: Serum  direct  bilirubin  provides  a  practical  adjunct  to  early  assessment  of  suspected appendicitis, supporting faster and more proportionate decisions-earlier escalation when overall risk is  high  and  safe  observation  when  it  is  low.  Because  testing  is  rapid,  inexpensive,  and  universally available,  integration  into  local  diagnostic  pathways  is  feasible,  including  in  resource-constrained settings.

The process progresses to suppurative  inflammation,  and-if  unchecked -transmural  necrosis  (gangrene)  with  either contained abscess/phlegmon or free perforation and peritonitis (1 ). texts.orig: Appendicitis  peaks  in  adolescence  and  young adulthood-approximately the second to fourth decades-yet it can occur at any age (3).  Fewer than  5%  of  cases  are  diagnosed  in  children under five years, whereas about 40% present in individuals during second and third decades of life (4) .  In  the  United  States,  the  estimated lifetime risk of appendicitis is ~8.6% in males and  ~6.7%  in  females. At  operation,  complicated appendicitis-for example gangrene, perforation, or periappendiceal abscess/ phlegmon-is reported in roughly 16.5-24.4% of cases (5).

texts.orig: Roughly 75-80% of hepatic blood flow comes via the portal vein, which delivers gut-derived bacteria,  endotoxin,  and  absorbed  solutes.  In complicated appendicitis, the bacterial/ endotoxin  load  entering  the  portal  circulation can outstrip hepatic clearance, producing sepsis-associated cholestasis and hepatocellular injury with a rise in serum bilirubin. In parallel, Kupffer cells/ macrophages release proinflammatory cytokines-notably TNF-α, IL-1, and IL-6-that impair canalicular excretion of conjugated bilirubin, further driving hyperbilirubinaemia (6-8).

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: Discussion
texts.text: Discussion

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Acute appendicitis represents the most frequent cause of acute abdominal pain, yet there remains no single laboratory investigation that can  confirm  the  diagnosis  with  certainty ( 10 ) . Diagnostic uncertainty occasionally arises because  appendicitis  does  not  always  present with  typical  clinical  features,  and  right  iliac fossa  pain  has  a  wide  range  of  differential causes,  more  so  in  women ( 11 ) . Failure  to recognize and treat appendicitis promptly may culminate in perforation with peritoneal involvement, which is associated with significant morbidity and longer inpatient recovery ( 12 ) . The  incidence  of  appendiceal perforation is on the rise, currently documented between 13-37%. These complications substantially  heighten  morbidity,  with  wound infection or peritonitis affecting nearly half of patients (47%), and mortality recorded at approximately  3% ( 13 ) . Therefore, there is growing interest in identifying reliable laboratory markers to support the diagnosis.

texts.orig: The present study was designed to investigate whether serum hyperbilirubinemia can serve as a reliable early predictor of complicated appendicitis. Our results demonstrated a clear and  consistent  association  between  elevated bilirubin levels and the presence of perforated or gangrenous appendicitis, thereby reaffirming the biomarker's diagnostic relevance.

texts.orig: The  mean  age  in  our  study  population  (400 patients) was 29.6±11.7 years. This is consistent with the quoted incidence of Appendicitis in the literature where it is most frequently  seen  in  patients  in  their  second through fourth decades of life ( 14 ) . In our study, age was a significant differentiator between the two groups. Patients with complicated appendicitis were older (mean age 32.4 ± 13.8 years) compared to those with simple appendicitis  (mean  age  28.3  ±  10.3  years, p=0.001). This aligns with Yuan et al., (2022) and Lapsa et al., (2021), who found that older patients are more likely to experience complicated appendicitis, often due to delayed diagnosis  or  atypical  symptom  presentation. Additionally, older patients may have reduced immune  response and other comorbidities, further complicating their ability to fight infection  and  preventing  early  resolution  of appendicitis ( 15 , 16 ) .

texts.orig: The gender distribution in this study was nearly equal, with 199 males (49.8%) and 201 females (50.2%).  There  was  no  significant  difference between the groups (p=0.41), showing a slight male predominance in both simple and complicated  appendicitis  cases. This  suggests that sex does not significantly impact the risk of complications in appendicitis, which contrasts with  findings  by  Kollias  et  al.,  (2024),  who reported a higher incidence of appendicitis and complications  like  perforation  or  gangrene  in males ( 17 ) .

texts.orig: The mean temperature for the study population (400 patients) was 37.7 ± 0.29°C. Patients with complicated  appendicitis  had  a  significantly higher temperature (38.1 ± 0.17°C) than those with simple appendicitis (37.6 ± 0.10°C, p<0.001). This suggests that fever may indicate severe infection or systemic inflammation, which are common in complicated appendicitis. Similarly, the mean pulse rate was 75.5 ± 10.7 bpm. The pulse was significantly higher in the complicated  appendicitis  group  (90.2  ±  3.6 bpm)  compared  to  the  simple  appendicitis group  (68.6  ±  3.6  bpm,  p<0.001).  Elevated pulse rates are typically seen in systemic infections,  reflecting  the  body's  response  to infection. Tachycardia, a common response to systemic  inflammation  or  sepsis,  was  more pronounced in complicated appendicitis cases. These findings align with Sasaki et al., (2020), who  reported  higher  body  temperature  and heart rate in patients with complicated appendicitis  (median  temperature  37.5  °C  vs 37.0 °C, p<0.001; median heart rate 85 vs 76 bpm, p<0.001), and a higher proportion meeting tachycardia criteria (≥100 bpm: 18.4% vs 5.6%, p=0.006)  (18) .

In our study, the duration of symptoms was significantly longer in patients with complicated appendicitis (61.6 ± 30.7  hours)  compared  to  those  with  simple appendicitis (17.6 ± 10.2 hours, p<0.001). This supports the notion that longer symptom duration is associated with more severe cases.

texts.orig: In  our  study,  WBC  counts  were  significantly higher in patients with complicated appendicitis (11.5  ±  2.9  ×10³/µL)  compared  to  simple appendicitis (7.6 ± 2.5 ×10³/µL, p < 0.001), and WBC  independently predicted complicated disease (OR 1.53, p < 0.001). WBC levels also correlated  with  bilirubin,  indicating  a  link  to inflammation  and  cholestasis  in  severe  cases. However, Emmanuel et al., (2011) found that hyperbilirubinemia had higher specificity than WBC or CRP for diagnosing appendicitis and its  complications ( 10 ) .  Giordano  et  al.,  (2013) confirmed  bilirubin's  usefulness  for  detecting perforation  but  noted  it  should  be  used  with other clinical data and laboratory data such as WBC  (20) ,  while  Birben  et  al.,.  (2021)  found elevated bilirubin helpful in diagnosing appendicitis even with normal WBC counts  (21 ).

texts.orig: Direct  bilirubin  showed  significant  positive correlations with clinical severity markers, including (duration r=0.32; temperature r=0.40; pulse r=0.45; WBC r=0.21). Notably, bilirubin did  not  correlate  with  systolic  blood  pressure (SBP) and showed only a minimal relationship with diastolic blood pressure (DBP, total bilirubin r=0.11). These findings align with the idea that bilirubin reflects systemic inflammation and cholestatic trends associated with severe illness.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: On adjusted logistic regression, direct bilirubin remained independent predictor of complicated appendicitis with very large effect sizes (direct OR  432.2,  95%  CI  92-1945;  both  p<0.001), over  and  above  age,  comorbidities,  symptom duration, temperature, pulse, and WBC (which were  themselves  significant).  Blood  pressure and sex were not retained. While the magnitude of the ORs reflects the strong separation created by  the  chosen  cut-offs,  the  key  point  is  that bilirubin  retains  predictive  value  even  after accounting  for  other  clinical  and  laboratory signals.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Practically, direct bilirubin >0.39 mg/dL should escalate concern for complication when combined with longer symptom duration, fever, tachycardia,  and  leukocytosis-all  of  which were significantly higher in complicated cases in  this  cohort.  Given  the  high  NPV  at  ≤0.39 mg/dL, low direct bilirubin can help deprioritize urgent operative or advanced imaging in otherwise low-risk presentations, while acknowledging that bilirubin is an adjunct, not a standalone decision tool. Direct bilirubin adds incremental  information  but-given  its  lower specificity-should  be  interpreted  alongside total bilirubin and the broader clinical picture.

texts.orig: Conclusion
texts.text: Conclusion

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This study demonstrates that serum  direct hyperbilirubinemia,  particularly  levels  ≥  0.39 mg/dL      is  a  strong  predictor  of  complicated appendicitis,  correlating  with  clinical  severity markers such as symptom duration, temperature, pulse, and WBC. Bilirubin testing, as  a  specific  "rule-in"  marker,  complements clinical  judgment  and  offers  a  cost-effective, easily  accessible  tool  for  early  diagnosis  and timely  intervention.  Our  findings  support  the incorporation of bilirubin into routine diagnostic pathways to improve decisionmaking,  optimize  resource  use,  and  reduce treatment delays.
